intro: Exponential functions describe things that grow or shrink by the same percent each step, like savings with interest or a cooling cup of tea. Logarithms are the reverse tool, answering "what power do I need?", and this branch uses both to solve real problems about growth, decay and scales like decibels.

IV.12.01.what: Understanding exponential growth: a quantity that is multiplied by the same number each step, like bacteria doubling every hour.

levels.a: Works out a growing amount by multiplying step after step.
levels.b: Uses a growth formula, starting amount times growth factor to the power x.
levels.c: Writes the formula from a starting amount and growth factor.
levels.d: Finds the starting amount and growth factor from a table.
levels.e: Finds the formula from two points on the curve.
levels.f: Finds a missing value from two others without working out the full formula.

IV.12.02.what: Understanding exponential decay: a quantity that shrinks by the same percent each step, like a car losing value.

levels.a: Tells growth from decay by whether the multiplier is above or below 1.
levels.b: Converts a decay multiplier, like 0.96, into a percent loss, like 4 percent.
levels.c: Finds the decay multiplier and percent loss from a table.
levels.d: Solves real problems, such as a car's value after several years.

IV.12.03.what: Graphing exponential functions and recognizing their shape: a curve that levels off on one side and shoots up or down on the other.

levels.a: Finds key points on an exponential graph.
levels.b: Describes the flat line the graph approaches on one side.
levels.c: Gives the allowed inputs and possible outputs.
levels.d: Tells a growth curve from a decay curve.
levels.e: Finds the growth factor from a point on the graph.
levels.f: Counts solutions of an equation by picturing two graphs, without solving.

IV.12.04.what: Shifting, flipping and stretching exponential graphs.

levels.a: Describes shifts up, down, left and right.
levels.c: Tracks how a point moves under a stretch and flip.
levels.d: Finds the new flat line the graph approaches and the new range.
levels.e: Finds three unknown numbers in the formula from three points.
levels.f: Shows that a stretch of an exponential graph is really a sideways shift.

IV.12.05.what: Writing growth and decay models from percent changes, like prices rising 3 percent a year.

levels.a: Turns a percent increase into a multiplier, such as 3 percent becoming 1.03.
levels.b: Turns a percent decrease into a multiplier, such as 3 percent becoming 0.97.
levels.c: Writes the full model from a starting amount and a percent rate.
levels.d: Converts a weekly rate into the equivalent yearly rate.

IV.12.06.what: Calculating compound interest, where interest is added to savings regularly and then earns interest itself.

levels.a: Uses the compound interest formula to find a final amount.
levels.b: Works out the rate per period and the number of periods, such as quarterly.
levels.c: Compares two savings offers to see which pays more.
levels.d: Finds how long money takes to reach a target, using logarithms.

IV.12.07.what: Meeting the number e, about 2.718, which arises when interest is compounded continuously and appears throughout science.

levels.a: Sees e emerge by compounding more and more often.
levels.b: Uses the continuous growth formula for money.
levels.c: Evaluates points on the graph of e to the power x.
levels.d: Uses continuous growth for populations and similar settings.
levels.e: Finds exact rates and times, such as a doubling time.
levels.f: Finds a limit value that turns out to be a power of e.

IV.12.08.what: Understanding a logarithm as the answer to "what power?": log base 3 of 243 asks what power of 3 gives 243.

levels.a: Finds a logarithm by asking which power gives the number.
levels.b: Uses the link between a logarithm statement and a power statement.
levels.c: Uses common logs (base 10) and natural logs (base e).
levels.d: Knows the log of 1 is 0 and the log of the base is 1, and that logs and powers undo each other.

IV.12.09.what: Switching between power form, such as 2 to the 4 equals 16, and logarithm form, log base 2 of 16 equals 4.

levels.a: Rewrites a power statement as a logarithm.
levels.b: Rewrites a logarithm as a power statement.
levels.c: Does the same with e and the natural log.
levels.d: Solves simple log equations by switching forms.

IV.12.10.what: Working out the value of logarithms, by hand when possible and by calculator otherwise.

levels.a: Evaluates logs of exact powers by hand.
levels.b: Evaluates logs whose answers are fractions or negative numbers.
levels.c: Estimates a log between two whole numbers.
levels.d: Uses a calculator for other logs.
levels.e: Evaluates logs involving roots and bases that are themselves powers.
levels.f: Multiplies a long chain of logs that collapses to one simple value.

IV.12.11.what: Using the log rules, which turn multiplying into adding, dividing into subtracting, and powers into multiplying.

levels.a: Uses the rule that the log of a product is a sum of logs.
levels.b: Uses the rule that the log of a quotient is a difference of logs.
levels.c: Uses the rule that the log of a power brings the power to the front.
levels.d: Expands one log into several, and combines several into one.

IV.12.12.what: Changing the base of a logarithm, which lets a calculator work out logs in any base.

levels.b: Evaluates a log in any base with a calculator.
levels.c: Explains why the formula works using power form.
levels.d: Compares the sizes of logs in different bases.

IV.12.13.what: Graphing logarithmic functions, which rise quickly at first and then ever more slowly.

levels.a: Sees the log graph as the mirror image of an exponential graph.
levels.b: Finds the upright line the graph approaches but never reaches.
levels.c: Tracks how points move under shifts and stretches.
levels.d: Finds the allowed inputs, which must keep the inside positive.
levels.e: Finds the base and shift from features of the graph.
levels.f: Solves an equation mixing a log and a straight line by spotting the single crossing.

IV.12.14.what: Solving exponential equations, where the unknown is in the power.

levels.a: Rewrites both sides with the same base when possible.
levels.b: Takes logs of both sides to bring the unknown down.
levels.c: Gets the power alone before taking logs.
levels.d: Gives both an exact answer and a decimal.
levels.e: Pulls out a shared power before solving.
levels.f: Solves an equation that is really a quadratic in 3 to the power x.

levels.a: Rewrites a log equation in power form to solve it.
levels.b: Combines logs into one first, then solves.
levels.c: Sets the insides equal when a log equals a log in the same base.
levels.d: Checks answers, rejecting any that make a log's inside zero or negative.
levels.e: Solves when logs have different bases.
levels.f: Solves an equation that is a quadratic in the log itself.

IV.12.16.what: Using half-life (time to halve) and doubling time to model decay and growth, such as carbon dating.

levels.a: Finds how much remains after a time, given the half-life.
levels.b: Finds how many there are after a time, given the doubling time.
levels.c: Finds the time taken to reach a given amount.
levels.d: Estimates the age of an old object by carbon dating.

IV.12.17.what: Using log scales, like decibels, pH and earthquake magnitudes, and fitting exponential models to data.

levels.a: Uses the formulas for pH and decibels.
levels.b: Compares earthquake sizes, where each step up means ten times the shaking.
levels.c: Uses a calculator to fit an exponential model to data.
levels.d: Takes logs of data to turn a curve into a straight line.
